items.title: Lupus nephritis: Pilot study expanding induction treatment options relying on oral dexamethasone as an alternative to parenteral pulse steroids.
items.abstract: BackgroundLupus nephritis (LN) affects over 60% of patients with systemic lupus erythematosus and is a risk factor for progression to end stage kidney disease. Guidelines recommend high dose parenteral methylprednisolone "pulses" for induction, although intravenous pulse therapy has not been rigorously compared to oral therapy. In this observational study, we report the outcomes of 17 patients who initiated therapy for LN with high dose oral dexamethasone.MethodsLN patients treated with oral dexamethasone between December 2021, and January 2025, were identified and baseline characteristics were recorded. Patients were assessed for a complete renal response (CRR, uPCR < 500, eGFR > 80%), satisfactory renal response (SRR, uPCR < 700, eGFR > 80%), or partial renal response (PRR, uPCR ≤ half of baseline uPCR, eGFR > 80%) at 1 year after receipt of dexamethasone. Responses were compared to outcomes in the BLISS-LN, AURORA and REGENCY trials.ResultsSeventeen patients with LN treated with induction dexamethasone were identified. The average age was 40 years old, and 15 patients were female. Six patients were of African ancestry, four Hispanic ethnicity, and three were White. Fourteen patients had proliferative LN. 47% of patients achieved a CRR, 59% obtained a SRR, and 53% obtained a PRR. Renal outcomes compared favorably to outcomes in the active arms of the BLISS-LN, AURORA 1, and REGENCY studies. Biomarkers including C3, C4, and dsDNA antibodies improved throughout the period. Proteinuria declined in 14 of 17 patients.ConclusionPatients with LN initially treated with oral dexamethasone in place of intravenous pulse methylprednisolone achieved responses similar to outcomes in recent LN trials. Dexamethasone is a promising potential oral option to initiate treatment for LN obviating need for parenteral therapy.

items.title: Association between IRAK1 gene rs1059703 polymorphism and rheumatoid arthritis risk.
items.abstract: This meta-analysis aimed to investigate the relationship between interleukin-1 receptor-associated kinase ( IRAK1 ) gene rs1059703 and rheumatoid arthritis (RA) risk. The pooled odds ratio (OR) and 95% confidence interval (95% CI) were calculated. Funnel plot with trim-and-fill analysis was used for publication bias investigation. IRAK1 gene rs1059703 was not significantly associated with RA risk under dominant genetic model (OR = 1.47, 95%CI = 0.96-2.24, p  = 0.071), recessive genetic model (OR = 1.14, 95%CI = 0.92-1.40, p  = 0.2258), allele genetic model (OR = 1.29, 95%CI = 0.95-1.75, p  = 0.0878), and codominant genetic model (OR = 1.33, 95%CI = 0.82-2.15, p  = 0.2125). Subgroup analysis also suggested that IRAK1 gene rs1059703 polymorphism was correlated with RA risk under dominant genetic model (I 2  = 80.9%, P Q  < 0.0001, OR = 1.77, 95%CI = 1.12-2.79, p  = 0.014) and allele model (I 2  = 79.6%, P Q  = 0.0002, OR = 1.45, 95%CI = 1.05-2.00, p  = 0.026) in Caucasian. Sensitivity analysis indicated that there was no significant change in the combined OR. No publication bias was observed. A statistically significant association between IRAK1 rs1059703 and RA risk was observed in Caucasian populations, but not in Asian populations with the available power under the current sample size. The apparent Caucasian association observed in the full dataset was not sustained after restricting analyses to HWE-compliant studies, where only a single Caucasian study remained.

items.title: Outcome measures and monitoring framework in juvenile systemic sclerosis: bridging routine care and clinical trials.
items.abstract: Juvenile systemic sclerosis (jSSc) is an orphan multisystem autoimmune disease that can cause significant morbidity during childhood and can lead to significant worsening of quality of life. The pathophysiological features are identical with adult-onset systemic sclerosis (SSc), jSSc exhibits a distinct clinical phenotype characterized by a significantly higher prevalence of diffuse cutaneous involvement, frequent overlap syndromes, distinct autoantibody profiles, and different long-term survival trajectories. Historically, the evaluation of jSSc has relied heavily on the extrapolation of adult outcome measures, which fail to account for developmental physiology, somatic growth, and pediatric-specific feasibility constraints. This review provides a comprehensive overview of indicators of disease activity and severity which might be used in daily clinical practice and adapted as outcome measures in future clinical trials. It includes global outcome measures, organ-specific outcomes (including skin, pulmonary, cardiac, gastrointestinal, musculoskeletal, renal, and vascular involvement), patient-reported outcome measures (PROMs), and clinician-reported outcomes (ClinROs). The performance of adult indices within pediatric cohorts are evaluated, if applicable. Additionally, we analyze severity scores like the Juvenile Systemic Sclerosis Severity Score (J4S) alongside modern consensus metrics derived from the international Hamburg symposia. We emphasize the integration of pediatric-adapted clinical assessments, quantitative imaging, and patient and physician related outcomes. The development of outcome measure in jSSc requires a paradigm shift from static severity scores to dynamic, multi-dimensional indicators capable of differentiating reversible inflammatory activity from potential permanent damage accrual. Validating pediatric-specific thresholds for physiological and cutaneous change remains an urgent priority. Over the next decade, the integration of artificial intelligence (AI)-driven quantitative imaging, decentralized home-based digital health tools, and molecular biomarkers probably will gain an essential role to optimize clinical trial readiness and personalize therapeutic strategies for children with systemic sclerosis. Not applicable.

items.title: Superior sagittal sinus thrombosis with intracranial hemorrhage in a patient on infliximab: a case report.
items.abstract: Superior sagittal sinus thrombosis (SSST) is a rare but life-threatening form of cerebral venous thrombosis. Although several prothrombotic and autoimmune conditions are recognized risk factors, SSST occurring in patients with rheumatoid arthritis (RA) receiving tumor necrosis factor-alpha (TNF-α) inhibitor therapy remains exceptionally rare and poorly described in the literature. We present a 59-year-old Caucasian female with RA treated with infliximab who developed extensive superior sagittal sinus thrombosis with concurrent intracranial and subarachnoid hemorrhage. The patient was managed with anticoagulation, blood pressure control, and seizure prophylaxis, with subsequent clinical and radiologic improvement at one-month follow-up. Hypercoagulability evaluation was overall unrevealing, and no other clear provoking etiology was identified. Given the rarity of this presentation, we report this case to raise awareness of a possible association between cerebral venous thrombosis and TNF-α inhibitor therapy in patients with rheumatoid arthritis. This is especially important given the increasing and widespread use of biologic agents in the treatment of autoimmune diseases.

items.title: Sex-specific outcomes in methotrexate therapy among patients with psoriatic arthritis and psoriasis.
items.abstract: The purpose of this paper is to identify sex-specific patterns in methotrexate (MTX) therapy among patients with psoriatic arthritis (PsA) and psoriasis (PsO). Data from adult patients treated with MTX monotherapy included in the Dutch southwest Early Psoriatic Arthritis Registry (rheumatology) or Continuous Assessment of Psoriasis Treatment Use REgistry with Methotrexate (dermatology) registries were obtained to create 2 cohorts of patients with PsA or PsO, respectively. Drug survival was assessed using Kaplan-Meier and Cox regression analyses. Disease activity, dosing, adverse events, and subsequent treatments were evaluated. A total of 525 (50.1% female) patients were included in the PsA cohort and 217 (41.1% female) patients in the PsO cohort. In the PsA cohort, female sex was associated with shorter drug survival (adjusted hazard ratio [HR] = 2.5; 95% CI, 1.6-4.1; P < .001), whereas in the PsO cohort, female sex was associated with longer drug survival (HR = 0.6; 95% CI, 0.4-0.9; P  = .008). Disease activity at MTX discontinuation was higher in females than males in the PsA cohort (Psoriatic Arthritis Disease Activity Score: 3.9 [1.0] vs 3.1 [1.5], P  = 0.037), whereas in the PsO cohort, disease activity was higher in males than females (Psoriasis Area and Severity Index: 4.8 [6.4] vs 3.5 [3.7], P  = .032). MTX dosing was comparable between sexes, though average doses were higher in the PsA than in the PsO cohort (18.2 [7.5] vs 15.0 [3.3] mg/wk, P < .001). Drug survival and treatment response of MTX vary between PsA and PsO, with females in the PsA cohort while males in the PsO cohort having worse outcomes.

items.title: Hospital Burden and Care Pathways of ANCA-Associated Vasculitis in Italy: A Focus on Clinical, Economic, and Geographic Dimensions.
items.abstract: Antineutrophil cytoplasmic antibody (ANCA)-associated vasculitides (AAVs) are rare autoimmune diseases characterized by heterogeneous clinical presentation and substantial morbidity. Evidence suggests high healthcare utilization and economic burden of ANCA-associated vasculitis (AAV), particularly owing to hospitalization as well as geographic variation in the organization of specialized care. However, national-level analyses examining outcomes, resource use, and geographic differences in care pathways remain limited. The study aimed to identify hospitalized patients with granulomatosis with polyangiitis (GPA) and microscopic polyangiitis (MPA) using administrative data, characterize their hospital burden and geographic care pathways in Italy, and investigate determinants of hospital costs and in-hospital mortality. Nationwide Italian hospital discharge records (2010-2019) were used to identify patients with GPA and MPA using International Classification of Diseases, Ninth Revision, Clinical Modification (ICD-9-CM)-based algorithms. Hospital resource use, costs, in-hospital mortality, inter-regional mobility, and continuity of specialized care were estimated. Determinants of hospital costs were analyzed using generalized linear models (gamma distribution and log link), and in-hospital mortality was analyzed using the Cox proportional hazards model. We identified 3763 patients with GPA and 1206 patients with MPA, with a mean of 6.9 and 8.6 admissions per patient, respectively, over 10 years. In-hospital mortality was 20.3% (GPA) and 21.4% (MPA), with over 70% of deaths occurring within 2 years of the first observed key diagnosis in hospital records. Mean cumulative observed hospital costs during 2010-2019 were substantial (€28,275 for GPA and €36,462 for MPA per patient), with around 60% of costs concentrated in the year of the first observed key diagnosis and adjacent years. Marked regional variation in care pathways was observed, with patients residing in southern regions frequently receiving AAV-related care in northern hospitals. Lower hospital loyalty (seeking AAV-related care in numerous hospitals) was more commonly observed in several southern regions. In regression analyses, infections were the strongest predictors of both higher costs and in-hospital mortality, while lower hospital loyalty was associated with substantially higher costs but not in-hospital mortality. Our analysis showed that hospitalized patients with AAV in Italy experienced substantial inpatient burden, frequent admissions, and high in-hospital mortality. Infections and renal involvement were strongly associated with both costs and in-hospital mortality. The observed regional differences in mobility patterns and continuity of specialized care suggest important geographic variation in AAV care pathways within the Italian hospital system. These findings may help inform efforts to improve the coordination and continuity of specialized AAV care.

items.title: Sustained Inhibition of Structural Damage Progression and Improvements in Disease Activity With Guselkumab in Biologic-Naïve Participants with Active and Erosive Psoriatic Arthritis: Results Through Week 48 of the Phase 3b Randomized, Double-Blind, Placebo-Controlled APEX Study.
items.abstract: In APEX, guselkumab, which binds to the IL-23p19 subunit and CD64 on IL-23-producing cells, demonstrated significant joint efficacy and inhibition of structural damage progression in participants with active and erosive PsA through Week (W)24; W48 findings are reported herein. The APEX modified full analysis set included 1020 biologic-naïve adults with active PsA (≥3 tender joints; ≥3 swollen joints; CRP ≥0.3mg/dL; ≥2 erosive joints) randomized to guselkumab every (Q)4W (N=273), guselkumab at W0,4 then Q8W (N=371), or placebo followed by guselkumab Q4W beginning at W24 (N=376). Outcomes through W48 included ACR20/50/70 response rates (using multiple/nonresponder imputation); least squares mean (LSM) change in PsA-modified van der Heijde-Sharp score (vdH-S); achievement of clinically meaningful improvement (CMI; ≥0.35-point) in HAQ-DI, ≥90% improvement in Psoriasis Area and Severity Index (PASI90), and minimal disease activity (MDA). Through W48, 93% (950/1020) of participants completed study intervention. Guselkumab Q4W and Q8W through W48 demonstrated durable ACR20/50/70 response rates (71-74%/51-56%/31-35%), and low rates of structural damage progression (vdH-S LSM change: 0.60-0.78); 60-64% of participants reported HAQ-DI CMI, 74-80% achieved PASI90, 36-41% achieved MDA. Following transition to guselkumab, structural damage progression among placebo-randomized participants diminished (vdH-S LSM change W0-24: 0.96; W24-48: 0.41) and clinical response rates increased through W48. Adverse event rates were consistent with placebo and guselkumab through W24 and stable through W48 of guselkumab. APEX W48 findings further support guselkumab use for durable and comprehensive treatment of diverse PsA manifestations. Inhibition of cumulative joint damage with guselkumab may optimize outcomes.

items.title: The association of gout flare resolution with physical activity and sleep: a prospective remote-monitoring study.
items.abstract: This study aimed to determine whether gout flare resolution is associated with physical activity and sleep. These findings were intended to inform the future development of a definition for flare resolution. Data from 81 participants with gout who experienced >1 flare during a 6-month prospective observational study were included. Daily activity (step count) and sleep (total sleep time and deep sleep percentage) were collected remotely using wrist-worn trackers. Daily flare occurrence was captured using smartphone diaries. Activity/sleep outcomes during each flare episode were compared to those during three resolution timeframes: T1: the first day following the flare; T2: the consecutive window immediately following the flare and equal in length to the flare; and T3: the consecutive window equal in length to the flare and immediately following a washout window (equal in length to the flare). Adjusted differences in medians between flare and resolution timeframes were estimated using linear quantile mixed models. Daily step count was lower during flares compared with all resolution timeframes (all P<0.033). T3 provided the best overall model fit, suggesting that resolution is most clearly distinguished from the flare when using this timeframe. No significant differences between flare and resolution were observed for the sleep outcomes for any resolution timeframe. Physical activity improves soon after flare cessation, with the clearest distinction between flare and resolution observed over a longer post-flare recovery period, whereas sleep metrics do not differentiate flare from resolution states. These findings support physical activity as a useful objective domain for gout flare resolution.

items.title: Single-cell analysis reveals CXCL16 + dendritic cells and clonally expanded GZMK + CD4 T cells driving joint inflammation in psoriatic arthritis.
items.abstract: Psoriatic arthritis (PsA) is a chronic immune-mediated arthritis affecting approximately 30% of individuals with psoriasis. The mechanisms driving PsA joint inflammation remain incompletely defined. To address this gap, we performed multimodal single-cell sequencing of immune cells from matched peripheral blood and synovial fluid (SF) from 6 PsA patients, with comparisons to a rheumatoid arthritis (RA) patient and 6 healthy controls (HC). SF CD4 and CD8 T cells displayed elevated expression of TOX, PDCD1, CTLA4, GZMK, CXCR3, and CXCR6, reflecting a tissue-specific activation state. CD4 T cell sub-clustering revealed clonally expanded populations enriched for GZMK and cytotoxic gene programs, suggesting antigen-driven activation. In contrast, CD8 T cell clonality showed a significant correlation with GZMK expression, however GZMK + CD8 T cells in the joint exhibited a transcriptional signature consistent with functional exhaustion. Concurrently, SF was enriched for CD141 + , CD1c + , CCR7 + , and SIGLEC6 + dendritic cells (DCs), characterized by increased CXCL16 expression and antigen presentation pathways. Flow cytometry and ELISA in an additional 25 PsA patients and 16 HCs confirmed protein-level enrichment of key chemokines and GZMK + T cells. Cell-cell communication analysis highlighted CXCR6-CXCL16 and CXCR3-CXCL10 chemokine axes as mediators of immune cell recruitment and retention, while in vitro assays showed enhanced migration of PsA SF T cells toward a CXCL16 gradient relative to paired blood. Together, these findings suggest that clonally expanded GZMK + CD4 T cells in PsA are cytotoxic and antigen-responsive, contributing to joint inflammation following recruitment by CXCL16-producing dendritic cells.

items.title: Tear-based biomarker trajectories associated with uveitis in juvenile idiopathic arthritis: a multicenter prospective study.
items.abstract: Extent of uveitis risk in juvenile idiopathic arthritis (JIA) is based on clinical factors. We aim to compare the trajectories of tear-based biomarker levels of patients with JIA with and without uveitis. This prospective multicenter study included children with JIA at risk for uveitis (JIA-no-U), and with JIA-associated uveitis (JIA-U). Serial tear samples were collected from each eye by Schirmer strips at enrollment (E) and follow-up (FU1, FU2). S100 proteins, cytokines, and chemokines were assayed by Luminex or ELISA and compared between groups. Fifty patients (37 JIA-no-U, 13 JIA-U) contributed 222 samples (150 JIA-no-U, 73 JIA-U). At E there were no significant differences in biomarker levels between JIA-U and JIA-no-U. During follow-up of JIA-U, monocyte chemoattractant protein-1 (MCP-1) levels increased longitudinally from E to FU1 and FU2 (1.63±0.31 to 2.46±0.31, p=0.005; and 2.89±0.32, p<0.0001), similar in Chemokine (C-X-C motif) Ligand (CXCL)-10 from E to FU1 and FU2 (4.39±0.41 to 5.26±0.41, p = 0.030; and 6.51±0.43, p < 0.0001) and in IL-8 levels from E to FU1 and FU2 (3.09±0.30 to 4.25±0.30, p = 0.006; and 4.65±0.32, p ≤ 0.001). In both groups, S100A12 and S100A8/A9 increased from E to FU. Longitudinal changes in MCP-1, CXCL10 and IL-8 levels in tear fluid in JIA-U may reflect inflammatory ocular processes and support the role of monocytes and interferon related pathways in uveitis. Lack of differences in S100 proteins may reflect systemic inflammation from arthritis. Tear-based biomarkers may support clinical factors for identifying children with JIA who develop uveitis.

items.title: Sema4A neutralization reduces fibrosis and inflammation in a mouse model of systemic sclerosis and a 3D model of immunity-driven fibrosis.
items.abstract: ﻿OBJECTIVE: We previously showed that Semaphorin4A (Sema4A) is elevated in patients with systemic sclerosis (SSc) and promotes inflammation and fibrosis in vitro. Here, we examined the effect of Sema4A neutralization in vivo and in 3D fibrosis models. Sema4A plasma levels were measured by ELISA in healthy controls (n=31) and patients with SSc (n=30). In the bleomycin SSc-model, mice were treated with an anti-Sema4A neutralizing antibody or its respective isotype control (n=6-7). The 3D fibrosis models, consisting of collagen hydrogel, dermal fibroblasts, and peripheral blood mononuclear cells, were stimulated with recombinant Sema4A, rapamycin, or antibodies neutralizing Sema4A, PlexinD1, PlexinB2, Neuropilin-1 or their respective isotype controls (n=6-10). Collagen content was determined by trichrome staining and hydroxyproline assay. Gene expression was determined by RT-qPCR and obtained from GEO-NCBI expression arrays, while protein expression by immunohistochemistry, immunoblotting and flow cytometry. Circulating Sema4A was elevated in patients with SSc (p<0.0001), while Sema4A receptors were elevated in SSc skin and lung (p ranged from <0.05 to 0.0001). Anti-Sema4A administration significantly reduced skin and lung collagen content in bleomycin-treated mice (p<0.01), as well as the expression of extracellular matrix components, fibrotic and inflammatory mediators, and immune cell infiltration. In the 3D models, SSc serum and SSc PBMCs induced cell contraction, which was drastically abrogated by blocking Sema4A (p<0.01). This effect was associated with reduced expression of fibrotic mediators and attenuated mTORC1 pathway activation. We confirmed the pro-fibrotic and pro-inflammatory role of Sema4A, postulating Sema4A neutralization as a novel approach for the treatment of SSc.

items.title: Current State of Allogeneic Hematopoietic Cell Transplantation for Still's Disease: A Collaborative Perspective from Attendees of the Systemic Juvenile Idiopathic Arthritis Foundation NextGen Conference.
items.abstract: Systemic juvenile idiopathic arthritis (sJIA) and adult-onset Still's disease (AOSD) represent a spectrum of Still's disease (SD) characterized by dysregulated innate immunity, severe systemic inflammation, and risk of life-threatening complications including macrophage activation syndrome (MAS) and associated lung disease (LD). Although IL-1 and IL-6 pathway inhibitors have improved outcomes, a subset of patients develop severe, refractory disease. This article summarizes the current evidence and multidisciplinary expert perspectives on the role of allogeneic hematopoietic cell transplantation (HCT) in refractory Still's disease. This Special Article is a conference summary based on presentations and multidisciplinary discussion at the 2024 Systemic JIA Foundation NextGen Conference, which convened an international, multidisciplinary group of rheumatologists, transplant physicians, immunologists, pulmonologists, and patient advocates. Recurrent MAS, progressive LD, persistent systemic inflammation despite IL-1/IL-6/JAK inhibition, and glucocorticoid dependence were identified as clinical features that may warrant consideration of allogeneic HCT in SD. Available data, mainly from small pediatric cohorts, suggest that allogeneic HCT can achieve clinical remission and improve pulmonary outcomes in select patients. However, transplant-related mortality remains substantial, particularly in patients with LD, and inflammatory disease may recur after HCT. HCT data in adults remain limited. Allogeneic HCT may be considered for select patients with severe, refractory SD, particularly those with recurrent MAS and/or progressive LD. Early multidisciplinary evaluation, shared decision-making, and careful patient selection are essential. Prospective multicenter studies and closer collaboration between pediatric and adult providers are needed to refine patient selection and improve outcomes.

items.title: Deep clinical renal response in lupus nephritis treated with belimumab: a real-world cohort study.
items.abstract: Lupus nephritis (LN) often progresses despite therapy, and current complete renal response (CRR) definitions tolerate residual proteinuria deemed suboptimal in other glomerulopathies. Belimumab, the first biologic approved for active LN, may enable deeper remission, but its real-world effectiveness is unknown. We retrospectively studied a single-centre cohort of biopsy-proven LN receiving add-on belimumab (2015-2025), with follow-up to 24 months and a paired-biopsy subgroup. We explored a study-specific stringent composite endpoint, deep clinical renal response (DCRR): urine protein-to-creatinine ratio (uPCR) <200 mg/g, absence of active glomerular haematuria and stable renal function, benchmarked against conventional CRR (uPCR <500 mg/g, stable renal function). Of 51 patients, 43 not in CRR at initiation were analysed. DCRR was achieved by 38.5% at 12 and 53.8% at 24 months, versus 66.7% and 76.9% for CRR, in available-case analysis; deep responses accrued gradually (median 17.7 vs 7.5 months), still increasing during the second year. Baseline uPCR was the only variable consistently associated with 12-month response. Renal response occurred alongside improvements in systemic activity, serological markers, and glucocorticoid exposure (SLEDAI-2K 13 to 2; anti-dsDNA 205 to 54 IU/mL and glucocorticoid reduction in 72%). In eight paired biopsies, activity index fell from 5.5 to 2 (p = 0.016) with attenuated glomerular C3 deposition (3+ to 1+, p = 0.031), whereas chronicity indices rose; these findings are exploratory given the small, uncontrolled sample. Deep renal response, accompanied by regression of histological activity, appears achievable in a growing proportion of patients. However, its impact on long-term renal protection remains to be established.

items.title: Contemporary issues relating to calcium pyrophosphate deposition disease.
items.abstract: Calcium pyrophosphate deposition (CPPD) disease is a common crystalline arthritis that has historically been under-studied compared to other rheumatic diseases including gout. For decades, the presence of CPPD in joints has been consider of uncertain clinical importance, with conflicting reports on whether CPPD leads to osteoarthritis progression or other adverse outcomes. A growing body of literature in the past five years has challenged the prevailing view of CPPD disease as "just chondrocalcinosis." These findings have arrived together with recent developments in classifying CPPD disease for research studies, advances in quantification of CPPD on imaging studies, consensus on outcomes to be measured in CPPD disease clinical trials, newly-identified genetic associations, and updates in the nomenclature for this crystalline arthritis. This review summarizes key updates in each of these realms.

items.title: Reasons-stratified treatment retention after JAK inhibitor discontinuation in rheumatoid arthritis: the ANSWER cohort study.
items.abstract: To compare the retention and disease activity trajectories of subsequent biologic and targeted synthetic disease-modifying antirheumatic drugs (b/tsDMARDs) after Janus kinase inhibitor (JAKi) discontinuation in patients with rheumatoid arthritis (RA). We analysed 500 treatment courses (TCs) from the ANSWER cohort in which subsequent b/tsDMARDs were initiated after JAKi discontinuation. Subsequent treatments were classified as TNF inhibitors (TNFi), anti-IL-6 receptor antibodies (aIL-6R), CTLA4-Ig and JAKi. Drug retention was stratified by the reason for prior JAKi discontinuation and evaluated using Kaplan-Meier and multivariable Cox analyses. Changes in Clinical Disease Activity Index (CDAI) over 12 months were analysed using mixed-effects models for repeated measures. After prior JAKi discontinuation due to ineffectiveness, CTLA4-Ig was associated with a significantly higher risk of discontinuation due to ineffectiveness than subsequent JAKi (HR 2.83, 95% CI 1.20-6.70). Among TCs in which the prior JAKi was discontinued due to toxic adverse events (AEs), TNFi and aIL-6R were associated with lower risks of toxic AE-related discontinuation than JAKi. Overall CTLA4-Ig was associated with higher risks of discontinuation due to ineffectiveness (HR 2.57, 95% CI 1.46-4.54) and total discontinuation excluding non-toxic reasons and remission (HR 1.77, 95% CI 1.02-3.07). CDAI trajectories over 12 months did not differ significantly between treatment groups. The optimal treatment strategy after JAKi discontinuation may depend on the reason for prior discontinuation. JAKi cycling, TNFi and aIL-6R may be reasonable after ineffectiveness, whereas after toxic AEs, TNFi and aIL-6R were associated with lower risks of subsequent toxic AE-related discontinuation than JAKi cycling.

items.title: Arterial Hypertension and Kidney Function Decline in Systemic Sclerosis and Sjögren's Disease: A Longitudinal Comparative Study.
items.abstract: Renal involvement is increasingly recognized in Systemic Sclerosis (SSc) and Sjögren's Disease (SjD). However, the association between hypertension and renal function decline in these conditions remains poorly understood. to compare renal function changes over time in patients with SSc and SjD; identify factors associated with clinically relevant renal function decline; and to evaluate whether the association between hypertension and renal function differs between the two diseases. We retrospectively analyzed patients with SSc and SjD, followed for up to 3 years. Renal function was assessed using estimated glomerular filtration rate (eGFR). Clinically relevant renal decline was defined as a reduction in eGFR ≥10 ml/min Multivariable logistic regression identified factors associated with renal function decline, including the interaction between diagnosis and hypertension. A total of 238 patients were included (114 with SSc and 124 with SjD), with a median age of 55 years (IQR 45-65) in SSc and 57 years (IQR 48-66) in SjD. At baseline, SSc patients showed higher eGFR compared to SjD, but experienced a greater decline over time (median -6 vs -2.1 ml/min, p < 0.05). Overall, 33.8% of patients developed clinically significant renal decline. In multivariable analysis, hypertension was independently associated with renal function decline (OR 10.01, 95% CI 3.51-28.56, p < 0.001), whereas diagnosis was not. A significant interaction between diagnosis and hypertension was observed (OR 6.56, 95% CI 1.03-41.69, p = 0.046), indicating a stronger association between hypertension and renal function decline in SSc than in SjD. In subgroup analyses, hypertension was significantly associated with renal decline in SSc but not in SjD. Hypertension was independently associated with renal function decline, with a stronger association in SSc than in SjD. These findings warrant confirmation in prospective studies. items.title: Exploring shared genetic architecture in psoriasis and rheumatoid arthritis: a multi-method approach.
items.abstract: Psoriasis and rheumatoid arthritis (RA) are immune-mediated diseases that co-occur clinically, but their shared genetic architecture and the direction of shared effects remain debated. We integrated genome-wide association study (GWAS) summary statistics from FinnGen and UK Biobank using linkage disequilibrium score regression (LDSC), high-definition likelihood (HDL), ρ-HESS, MTAG, CPASSOC, colocalization, and MAGMA. The primary cross-population analysis showed a negative global genetic correlation (LDSC unconstrained: rg = - 0.3004, P = 6.70 × 10⁻³; constrained: rg = - 0.2251, P = 3.00 × 10⁻⁴; HDL: rg = - 0.3307, P = 1.14 × 10⁻³). Ancestry-matched sensitivity analyses produced positive but heterogeneous estimates (FinnGen: rg = 0.2422 to 0.6334; UK Biobank: rg = 0.1294 to 0.3777) that were not uniformly significant. Cross-trait analyses identified 95 independent SNPs and 10 additional shared loci. After allele harmonization, all 10 loci showed opposite MTAG effect directions for psoriasis and RA (two-sided exact binomial P = 1.95 × 10⁻³), indicating directional heterogeneity and possible antagonistic pleiotropy. Colocalization provided evidence for a shared causal signal at two TYK2 variants, rs11085727 and rs144309607 (PP.H4 > 0.8; r² = 0.0805 and D' = 1.0), although these results should be interpreted cautiously because they may reflect distinct correlated variants. MAGMA identified immune-related tissue enrichment for psoriasis but not RA. Collectively, these findings indicate that psoriasis and RA share genetic loci, but the global direction of genetic correlation is ancestry- and data-source-dependent and that locus-level effects include opposing directions. TYK2 remains a plausible shared target, but its therapeutic implications require direction-aware fine-mapping and functional validation.

items.title: A gut microbiota-metabolite-host gene score for subtyping and predicting the treatment response in rheumatoid arthritis: integrative analysis with in silico knockout validation.
items.abstract: The pathogenesis of rheumatoid arthritis (RA) involves a complex interplay between immune dysregulation and metabolic disturbance, with the gut microbiota and its metabolites playing pivotal roles. However, integrated biomarkers based on the "gut microbiota-metabolite-host gene" regulatory axis that can quantify its impact on RA stratification and therapeutic response are lacking. We integrated multiple RA transcriptomic datasets to screen for host genes explicitly associated with the gut microbiota and metabolites using the gutMGene database. A gut microbiota-metabolite-host score (GMS) was constructed via principal component analysis (PCA). Immune infiltration patterns were evaluated using CIBERSORT. Furthermore, scRNA-seq was employed to map the cellular origins of key genes, and in silico knockout analysis using scTenifoldKnk was performed to simulate the functional ablation of core host genes within this regulatory axis. Additionally, molecular docking was conducted to validate the binding affinities between the key host proteins and the optimal small molecule. We identified seven microbiota-metabolite-host hub genes (FOS, JUN, IDO1, PEMT, EGFR, ABCC4, and FADS3) and constructed the GMS. The GMS stratified patients with RA into two distinct functional subtypes: an adaptive immune activation subtype and an inflammatory-metabolic composite subtype. Notably, the GMS demonstrated superior performance in predicting responses to anti-TNF and rituximab therapies. The scRNA-seq analysis revealed high expression of FOS and JUN in T cells and NK cells. In silico knockout analysis further revealed the central transcription factors FOS and JUN as key executors of this axis, as their ablation significantly affected osteoclast differentiation and the enrichment of TNF/MAPK inflammatory pathways. These computational findings support the core mechanism by which gut microbiota-metabolite signalling drives RA joint pathology via FOS/JUN. Molecular docking results confirmed strong binding interactions between the identified active molecules and their respective target proteins. This study establishes a GMS based on the gut microbiota-metabolite-host gene regulatory axis as a robust tool for molecular subtyping and predicting biological therapy responses in patients with RA. Crucially, through integrated computational modelling, including in silico knockout and molecular docking validation, we identified FOS/JUN as critical executor genes linking the gut microenvironment to RA bone destruction, providing novel targets for therapeutic strategies aimed at the gut-joint axis.

items.title: Sodium-glucose cotransporter 2 inhibitors in patients with systemic lupus erythematosus and lupus nephritis: A systematic review and meta-analysis.
items.abstract: IntroductionSystemic Lupus Erythematosus (SLE) and lupus nephritis (LN) carry substantial cardiorenal risks. Conventional immunosuppressive therapies primarily target inflammation but leave a burden of residual renal and metabolic damage. Sodium-glucose cotransporter 2 inhibitors (SGLT2i) provide clear cardiorenal protection in general populations, but data specific to SLE remains limited. This systematic review and meta-analysis evaluated the efficacy and safety of SGLT2i in patients with SLE and LN.MethodsComprehensive searches across five electronic databases (PubMed, Cochrane CENTRAL, Web of Science, Embase, and Scopus) were conducted up to April 2026 to identify randomized controlled trials (RCTs) and observational studies assessing SGLT2i in adult SLE/LN patients. Random-effects meta-analyses were performed to synthesize cardiorenal and safety outcomes using R Software.ResultsSix studies published between 2024 and 2025 were included. Pooled data demonstrated that SGLT2i use was associated with a significant improvement in estimated glomerular filtration rate (eGFR) compared to controls (MD: 4.02; 95% CI: 1.39-6.65; I 2 = 60.1%). SGLT2i significantly reduced the risks of progression to end-stage kidney disease (RR: 0.37; 95% CI: 0.25-0.56; I 2 = 11.0%), heart failure development (RR: 0.65; 95% CI: 0.56-0.75; I 2 = 0.0%), incident lupus nephritis (RR: 0.58; 95% CI: 0.44-0.76; I 2 = 0.0%), and re-hospitalizations (RR: 0.67; 95% CI: 0.57-0.79; I 2 = 0.0%). Furthermore, a significant reduction in all-cause mortality was observed (RR: 0.55; 95% CI: 0.36-0.86; I 2 = 76.2%). SGLT2i treatment demonstrated an acceptable safety profile across the included cohorts. The certainty of evidence for these findings was rated as low to very low, and results remain vulnerable to residual confounding from variables such as disease activity, corticosteroid burden, and immunosuppressive regimen.ConclusionPreliminary exploratory evidence suggests potential associations between SGLT2 inhibitors and cardiorenal outcomes in lupus nephritis. Given the low certainty of evidence and vulnerability to residual confounding from disease-specific variables, these hypothesis-generating findings require confirmation in well-designed randomized controlled trials.

items.title: Distinct trajectories of disease severity progression in juvenile systemic sclerosis.
items.abstract: Juvenile systemic sclerosis (JSSc) often presents with overlapping features, making phenotypic classification and disease progression difficult to define. This study investigated whether JSSc comprises latent disease severity subgroups with distinct longitudinal trajectories and examined baseline predictors of class membership. Retrospective cohort study using prospectively collected data from 45 patients with JSSc between January 2005 and December 2024. Demographic, clinical, laboratory, and disease severity data were collected. The primary outcome was progression-free survival (PFS), defined as percentage change in the Juvenile Systemic Sclerosis Severity score (J4S) over time. A Growth Mixture Model identified latent disease severity classes with distinct longitudinal trajectories and their baseline predictors. Thirty-eight JSSc patients (66% females), followed for ≥48 months, entered the study. PFS remained high in the fibrotic and limited cutaneous JSSc subtypes (80-100%) over the observation period, whereas the diffuse and sine scleroderma subtypes showed marked deterioration, with PFS decreasing to 54% and 25%, respectively. We identified two latent classes of disease severity: Class 1 showed low severity and good treatment response, Class 2 showed an active, progressive course with poor long-term outcomes. Baseline predictors of poor outcome were J4S >7.5, treatment initiation >9 months from disease onset, and >1.5 organs involved. Latent trajectory classes showed good concordance with JSSc clinical subtypes (κ = 0.660). We identified two latent classes of disease severity in JSSc with clear prognostic significance. High baseline J4S, delayed treatment, and greater organ involvement predicted a more severe disease course, paving the way for precision health strategies and optimized.

items.title: Activated B cells steer fibroblasts towards a proinflammatory phenotype in giant cell arteritis.
items.abstract: Giant cell arteritis (GCA) is characterized by chronic large-vessel inflammation and remodelling. Within affected arteries, especially in aorta, organized B cell clusters are mainly localized in adventitia, where fibroblasts represent the dominant stromal population. This study aims to investigate fibroblast heterogeneity within these clusters and B cell-fibroblast interactions in vitro as possible contributors to disease chronicity in GCA. Fibroblast phenotypes in CD20+B cell clusters in GCA and atherosclerotic aortic tissues were characterized using immunohistochemistry for fibroblast markers (CD90, PDPN, FAP, CD248, α-SMA) and cytokine expression (IL-6, GM-CSF, BAFF). In vitro, peripheral blood B cells from treatment-naïve GCA patients and healthy donors were stimulated and cocultured with human aortic adventitial fibroblasts (HAoAFs) using either direct cell coculture or transwell systems. To identify relevant molecular pathways for B cell-fibroblast interaction, HAoAFs were pre-treated with infliximab, tocilizumab, baricitinib or upadacitinib, followed by exposure to activated B cell conditioned medium (aBCCM). Protein secretion was assessed by ELISA, Luminex and Olink, mRNA expression was determined by qPCR. CD90+PDPN+immunofibroblasts mainly localized centrally, whereas CD90+FAP+ and CD90+CD248+fibroblasts mostly located at the border of the clusters. Fibroblasts in/around clusters co-expressed IL-6, GM-CSF, and BAFF. In vitro, HAoAFs cocultured with activated B cells or supernatants thereof upregulated IL-6, GM-CSF, PDPN, and FAP mRNA, and actively secreted IL-6, GM-CSF and BAFF, while type I collagen expression was suppressed. JAK-STAT inhibition abrogated these pro-inflammatory effects, whereas TNF-α and IL-6 receptor blockade did not. Activated B cells drive fibroblasts toward a pro-inflammatory phenotype, potentially sustaining chronic inflammation and disease progression in GCA. JAK-STAT signalling appears central to this effect, highlighting its therapeutic potency at the vascular level in GCA.

items.title: Single-cell eQTL Mendelian randomization reveals the monocyte-associated PRKCB-CTSL axis as a candidate regulatory pathway and potential therapeutic target in rheumatoid arthritis.
items.abstract: Rheumatoid arthritis (RA) involves persistent immune dysregulation, but cell-specific genetically regulated pathways remain unclear. We integrated cell-specific genetic and multi-omics evidence to prioritize candidate regulatory pathways. cis-eQTLs from 17 immune-cell populations were integrated with RA GWAS data by two-sample Mendelian randomization. Transcriptomics, WGCNA, and machine-learning feature selection identified convergent candidates. Single-cell and virtual perturbation analyses assessed cellular localization and downstream changes. Molecular docking and dynamics computationally prioritized compounds, and knockdown/rescue experiments evaluated the PRKCB-CTSL relationship. Eleven candidates had convergent genetic and transcriptomic support. PRKCB was retained by LASSO, SVM, and random forest and preferentially expressed in monocytes. Virtual perturbation implicated CTSL and antigen-processing/presentation pathways. PRKCB knockdown reduced CTSL expression and NF-κB phosphorylation, whereas CTSL restoration partially rescued NF-κB phosphorylation. Separately, structure-based analyses computationally prioritized ursodiol for the most favorable predicted PRKCB interaction among evaluated compounds. Genetic, transcriptomic, single-cell, computational, and in vitro evidence supports monocyte-associated PRKCB-CTSL as a candidate regulatory pathway in RA. Further mechanistic and in vivo studies are required to establish its causal and pharmacological relevance. Key Points • Multi-omics analysis identified 11 key RA-associated targets. • RA was classified into two molecular subtypes with distinct immune features. • PRKCB was identified as the core target enriched in monocytes. • The PRKCB-CTSL axis may drive RA inflammation, and ursodiol showed therapeutic potential.

items.title: Icotrokinra, a Targeted Oral Peptide, in Participants With Moderate-to-Severe Plaque Psoriasis and Self-Reported Psoriatic Arthritis: Results From a Pooled Analysis of the Phase 3 ICONIC-LEAD, ICONIC-ADVANCE 1, and ICONIC-ADVANCE 2 Trials.
items.abstract: Icotrokinra, a targeted oral peptide that precisely blocks the interleukin-23 receptor, is approved to treat adult and pediatric (≥12 years, ≥40 kg) patients with moderate-to-severe plaque psoriasis (PsO). Assess psoriatic arthritis (PsA)-specific outcomes through Week (W) 16 in a subgroup of phase-3 study participants with moderate-to-severe plaque PsO and self-reported medical history of PsA (PsO+PsA). Post-hoc analyses pooled data from ICONIC-LEAD and ICONIC-ADVANCE 1 and 2 among PsO+PsA participants randomized to once-daily icotrokinra 200 mg or placebo through W16. PsA-specific outcomes included mean change from baseline and ≥50% improvement in Patient's Global Assessment (PtGA) of PsA disease activity and Patient's Assessment of PsA Pain, and percent change from baseline in modified Nail Psoriasis Severity Index (mNAPSI). P values are nominal. Analyses included 216 participants (149 icotrokinra, 67 placebo). At W8, icotrokinra-treated participants reported greater improvements vs placebo in PtGA of PsA disease activity (-18.5 vs -4.8; P < 0.001) and PsA Pain (-17.1 vs -4.6; P < 0.001), with improvement sustained at W16 (-19.2 vs -0.8; P < 0.001; -19.5 vs -7.8; P = 0.003). At W16, greater proportions of icotrokinra-treated vs placebo-treated participants achieved ≥50% improvement in PtGA of PsA disease activity (47.0% vs 10.7%; P < 0.001) and PsA Pain (45.5% vs 16.1%; P < 0.001). At W16, icotrokinra improved mNAPSI by 41.6% (vs 118.6% worsening with placebo; P < 0.001). Adverse event rates were similar between icotrokinra and placebo. Icotrokinra demonstrated early, substantial improvements in participant-reported PsA activity and PsA Pain, and nail psoriasis, with a favorable safety profile through W16 in participants with PsO+PsA.

items.title: Mitochondrial Metabolic Reprogramming in Macrophages: A Key Driver of Rheumatoid Arthritis.
items.abstract: Rheumatoid arthritis (RA) is a chronic autoimmune disease characterized by persistent synovitis and progressive cartilage and bone destruction. Synovial macrophages are central coordinators of inflammatory signaling, stromal activation, and osteoclastogenesis, yet their pathogenic functions cannot be explained by extracellular cytokine networks alone. Increasing evidence indicates that macrophage activation is coupled to cell-intrinsic mitochondrial metabolic reprogramming. Within the hypoxic, nutrient-variable, and inflammatory RA synovium, macrophages undergo coordinated changes in glycolysis and oxidative phosphorylation, tricarboxylic acid cycle flux, mitochondrial reactive oxygen species production, fission-fusion dynamics, mitophagy, and mitochondrial DNA homeostasis. These alterations reshape bioenergetics while generating metabolites and organelle-derived danger signals that engage hypoxia-inducible factor 1α, nuclear factor-κB, the NOD-like receptor family pyrin domain-containing 3 inflammasome, and cyclic GMP-AMP synthase-stimulator of interferon genes signaling. The resulting metabolic-inflammatory circuits can stabilize pathogenic macrophage states and propagate inflammation to fibroblast-like synoviocytes, endothelial cells, and osteoclast-lineage cells. This review integrates current evidence on macrophage heterogeneity, mitochondrial remodeling, and intercellular signaling in RA. We further evaluate mitochondria-targeted antioxidants, metabolic modulation, restoration of mitochondrial quality control, inhibition of mitochondrial danger-signal sensing, and multistage nanodelivery. Particular emphasis is placed on evidence strength, macrophage-subset specificity, and the distinction between disease-driving abnormalities and compensatory adaptations. Finally, we outline the biomarkers, human-tissue validation, spatial multi-omics, and delivery strategies required to translate macrophage mitochondrial immunometabolism into precision therapy for RA.

items.title: Blood pressure variability associates with mortality risk of patients with ANCA-associated vasculitis.
items.abstract: Antineutrophil cytoplasmic antibody-associated vasculitis (AAV) is associated with increased cardiovascular risk, related to persistent inflammation and endothelial dysfunction. Long-term systolic blood pressure variability (SBPV), reflecting vascular damage, may predict outcomes better than mean blood pressure (BP). We investigated the impact of BP control and visit-to-visit BP variability (VVV), on all-cause mortality in AAV patients during maintenance therapy. We retrospectively studied 95 AAV patients followed at three Italian nephrology centers. SBPV was defined as the standard deviation of ≥4 systolic BP measurements within 12 months from the first SBPV assessment. Patients were stratified by SBPV tertiles. The primary outcome was all-cause mortality. Over a median follow-up of 78 months, 14 patients (14.7%) died. Deceased patients were older and had higher pulse pressure (PP) and VVV. Hypertension prevalence increased across SBPV tertiles (35%, 62%, 69%; P  = .02). Mortality rose from 6% in the lowest to 34.5% in the highest SBPV tertile (Fisher's exact, P  = .001). Time-averaged systolic BP was not associated with mortality. Conversely, each 5-mmHg increase in SBPV was associated with a two-fold higher risk of death [hazard ratio (HR) 2.03, 95% confidence interval (CI) 1.29-3.20; P  = .002]. SBPV remained significantly associated with outcome after full multi-variable adjustment, including age, sex, myeloperoxidase positivity, estimated glomerular filtration rate, PP, and proteinuria (adjusted HR 8.06 per 1 mmHg, 95% CI 1.42-45.54; P  = .02). In AAV patients, increased VVV was associated with all-cause mortality outperforming mean systolic BP. Further research is needed to confirm the impact of variable blood pressure on patient outcomes in AAV.

items.title: RNA therapeutics in rheumatoid arthritis, systemic lupus erythematosus, and systemic sclerosis: a compartment-aware translational framework.
items.abstract: Rheumatoid arthritis (RA), systemic lupus erythematosus/lupus nephritis (SLE/LN), and systemic sclerosis (SSc) remain major causes of chronic inflammation, disability, organ damage, and treatment burden despite therapeutic advances. RNA therapeutics offer programmable transcript suppression, network-level microRNA modulation, transient restoration of protective proteins, and targeting-ligand functions. Existing reviews largely catalogue modalities or individual delivery systems; this review instead asks whether a candidate forms an interpretable translational program across target biology, disease compartment, intended cell, productive intracellular access, direct target engagement, pathway pharmacodynamics, repeat-dose safety, and manufacturing feasibility. RA is primarily a synovial immune-stromal delivery problem in which RNA programs must also demonstrate an advantage over effective biologic or targeted synthetic therapies. SLE/LN offers interferon, B-cell, co-stimulatory, microRNA, messenger RNA (mRNA), and complement opportunities, but therapeutic nucleic acids and carriers must not intensify nucleic-acid sensing, interferon activity, or complement-associated injury. SSc combines strong antifibrotic RNA biology with an accessible skin proof-of-mechanism window, whereas lung, vascular, and internal-organ programs remain more delivery-limited. We separate human pathway validation, RNA-platform evidence outside the target disease, disease-specific RNA evidence, and patient efficacy. Recent human complement-factor-B pharmacodynamic data strengthen the platform-level evidence but do not establish efficacy in RA or LN. The most informative early trials will therefore be biomarker-enriched and mechanism-rich, with prespecified criteria that distinguish target failure from delivery, dose, endotype, or safety failure.

items.title: Targeting pathogenic immune cells in rheumatoid arthritis: emerging immunotherapeutic frontiers.
items.abstract: Rheumatoid arthritis (RA) is a persistent autoimmune condition that predominantly affects the joints resulting in inflammation, pain and progressive disability. Immunological imbalance, especially the stimulation of pathogenic immune cells, including T and B cells, macrophages, amongst others, is the cause of the disease, as it is critical to the development of the disease. The limitation of traditional anti-RA medications, such as non-steroidal anti-inflammatory drugs (NSAIDs) and disease-modifying anti-rheumatic drugs (DMARDs), in the treatment of the disease led to the development of more specific medicines. One of the most promising biologic agents, including monoclonal antibodies, cytokine inhibitors and cell-based therapies, are specifically targeting immune cells and inflammatory pathways in RA. This review examines these new immunotherapies, their mechanisms of action, clinical efficacy, and challenges associated with them, including resistance to treatment, safety issues, and the necessity to use personalised therapy. Also, the new immunotherapeutic approaches, which include targeting autoantibodies, gene therapy, and precision medicine, are promising new approaches that could result in more effective and personalised treatments. Finally, the review concludes with a discussion of future directions, where in combination therapies, next-generation biologics, and personalised treatment regimens are also possible and can change the way RA can be managed in the future. To preserve analytical depth, this review explicitly distinguishes established (regulatory-approved) therapies from investigational and experimental approaches and indicates the level of clinical evidence for each.

items.title: Biological sex and disease architecture in systemic sclerosis: a multilayer translational framework for precision medicine.
items.abstract: Biological sex is routinely incorporated into systemic sclerosis (SSc) research as a demographic or stratification variable. Women are substantially more likely to develop SSc, whereas men experience a greater burden of severe organ involvement and adverse outcomes. Whether these observations represent parallel sex-associated differences or reflect differences in the relationships among disease components remains unresolved. Here, we propose the Systemic Sclerosis-Multilayer Architecture Framework (SSc-MAF) as a hypothesis-generating framework for addressing this distinction. We define a sex-dependent architectural difference not as an isolated difference in a molecule, cell population, pathway, or clinical phenotype, but as a reproducible sex-associated difference in relationships among disease components, including multicellular communication, fibrovascular coupling, spatial tissue organization, molecular co-activation, or longitudinal clinical-biological trajectories. SSc-MAF therefore distinguishes clinical disease trajectories from the biological architecture that may generate them and from the methodological strategies required for empirical validation. We critically evaluate current evidence across immune, fibrovascular, metabolic, and regulatory domains, while distinguishing direct sex-stratified SSc evidence from indirect mechanistic evidence and framework-level hypotheses. We further outline measurable predictions and conditions that would weaken or fail to support individual propositions of SSc-MAF. This framework is intended not to establish sex-dependent disease architecture as a proven feature of SSc, but to provide an operational strategy for testing whether biological sex contributes information beyond conventional component-level comparisons and additive covariate adjustment.

items.title: Early recognition of eosinophilic granulomatosis with polyangiitis in outpatient settings: musculoskeletal and gastrointestinal clues beyond respiratory disease.
items.abstract: Eosinophilic granulomatosis with polyangiitis (EGPA) is a multisystem immune-mediated disease characterized by adult-onset asthma, eosinophilic inflammation, and necrotizing vasculitis of small-to-medium-sized vessels. Diagnosis is frequently prompted by clinically overt neurological, cardiac, renal, cutaneous, or gastrointestinal involvement. However, potentially informative manifestations may already be recognizable earlier, particularly when asthma, chronic rhinosinusitis with nasal polyps, and blood eosinophilia coexist with otherwise nonspecific extrapulmonary findings. Most cohorts describe manifestations at diagnosis or during established disease and provide limited information on their early temporal appearance across different specialties. This gap is particularly relevant to arthralgia and myalgia, which are common but poorly characterized, and to eosinophilic gastrointestinal manifestations that may initially be classified as organ-restricted eosinophilic gastrointestinal disorders. Biopsy-proven myositis is rare but has occasionally been reported at presentation or before clinically recognizable neuropathy. This review examines early and potentially recognizable manifestations of EGPA across outpatient settings, with particular attention to musculoskeletal symptoms, objective muscle involvement, eosinophilic gastrointestinal disease, and the therapeutic implications of distinguishing organ-restricted eosinophilic disease from systemic EGPA.

items.title: Integrating transcriptomic analysis to explore biomarkers and therapeutic targets for rheumatoid arthritis: a case-control and systems biology approach.
items.abstract: Rheumatoid Arthritis (RA) is a highly variable and unpredictable autoimmune disease, relying solely on physical symptoms often leads to delayed treatment and irreversible joint destruction. Therefore, identifying biomarkers in RA is necessary to bridge the gap between a patient's unique biological profile and successful clinical management. This study aims to identify distinct molecular signatures in RA patients by integrating systems biology and case-control methodologies. Transcriptomic datasets from various sources specifically synovial tissues, macrophages, blood, T-cells, natural killer T-cells, natural killer cells, neutrophils, and monocytes were analysed. Differentially Expressed Genes and functional enrichment pathways were identified, followed by Weighted Gene Co-expression Network Analysis to pinpoint hub genes. Machine learning models were used to extract consensus biomarkers. Two of the predicted biomarkers IL2RG) and Interferon-Gamma (IFNG) were further validated using an Enzyme-Linked Immunosorbent Assay (ELISA) in RA patient serum samples. The analysis revealed that synovial tissues and synovial macrophages exhibited pronounced transcriptomic expression changes. Six consensus biomarkers such as IFNG, PTEN, IL2RG, CDKN2D, VEGFA, and CDKN1A were computationally prioritized in synovial macrophages. Among these, IL2RG and IFNG were selected for preliminary experimental validation by ELISA. IL2RG concentrations were significantly higher in RA patients (1.34 ± 0.11 ng/mL) than in healthy controls (0.83 ± 0.07 ng/mL), while IFNG levels showed only a marginal increase (1.91 ± 0.06 pg/mL) compared to controls (1.69 ± 0.06 pg/mL). By integrating multi-tissue transcriptomic profiling with machine learning, this study mapped critical molecular changes in RA and prioritized six consensus biomarkers within synovial macrophages. Experimental validation confirmed that IL2RG and IFNG are significantly elevated in RA patients compared to healthy controls. These findings offer a promising, minimally invasive molecular markers for diagnosis and personalized clinical management in RA.

items.title: The application of Chicago classification 4.0 in esophageal motility disorders of scleroderma: a case-control study in China.
items.abstract: Systemic sclerosis (SSc) is a rare autoimmune connective tissue disease characterized by multi-organ fibrosis and vasculopathy that frequently involves the esophagus. This study assessed esophageal motility disorders in patients with SSc using High-resolution manometry (HRM) and classified these disorders according to the Chicago Classification version 4.0, aims to investigate the associations between esophageal dysfunction and clinical phenotypes in Chinese SSc patients, while exploring potential modifications to enhance the applicability of the Chicago v4.0 protocol in SSc patients. We retrospectively identified SSc patients fulfilling 2013 ACR criteria who underwent HRM classified by Chicago v4.0 at our center (2021-2023). Demographics, organ involvement, pulmonary-function tests, echocardiography and reflux symptom scores (RDQ/GERDQ) were extracted from the hospital information system; age and sex matched non-SSc HRM subjects served as controls. Associations between Chicago categories and clinical variables were examined by multinomial logistic regression. In our study, esophageal motility disorders were present in 76.7% of patients with systemic sclerosis, predominantly characterized by ineffective esophageal motility (IEM) (35%) and absent contractility (AC) (36.67%). The occurrence rate of AC rose with age. Symptoms of gastroesophageal reflux were more common in the AC group [Odds Ratio: 3.23 (1.02-10.22) vs 1.43(0.52-3.95), P<0.05, E value=2.99]. Diffusion capacity for carbon monoxide (DLCO) was significantly reduced in both IEM and AC (-2.03 vs -2.70, P value<0.05), with a more pronounced decrease in AC. Total lung capacity (TLC) and forced expiratory volume in one second (FEV1) exhibited stronger associations with AC (-1.04 and -0.8 respectively, p value<0.05). Upright HRM revealed more marked decreases in EGJ pressure and distal contractile integral (DCI) relative to the supine position in SSc patients, indicating that esophageal abnormalities may be more readily apparent during upright examination. Esophageal motility disorders in SSc were common and significantly associated with older age, gastroesophageal reflux symptoms, and reduced lung function. Future studies are needed to clarify whether early esophageal motility disorders are associated with disease progression and prognosis in patients.

items.title: Efficacy and safety of intravenous immunoglobulin in systemic sclerosis: a systematic review and meta-analysis.
items.abstract: Systemic sclerosis (SSc) is a complex autoimmune disease mainly characterized by progressive fibrosis affecting the skin and internal organs. Although several immunosuppressive and targeted therapies are currently available, many patients continue to experience refractory manifestations. Intravenous immunoglobulin (IVIG) has been increasingly used as an adjunctive treatment in selected cases; however, its efficacy across different disease manifestations remains incompletely defined. To systematically evaluate the efficacy and safety of IVIG in patients with systemic sclerosis and to quantitatively synthesize available evidence regarding its effects on skin involvement, gastrointestinal manifestations, and inflammatory myopathy. A systematic review and meta-analysis were conducted according to PRISMA 2020 guidelines. MEDLINE/PubMed, Embase, LILACS, and the Cochrane Library were searched from January 1966 to May 2026. Studies evaluating IVIG in adult patients with systemic sclerosis were included. Randomized controlled trials, observational cohorts, pilot studies, and case series were eligible. Quantitative synthesis was performed using random-effects models and standardized mean differences (SMDs) with 95% confidence intervals (CIs). Eleven studies were included in the systematic review. Six studies provided sufficient quantitative data for the meta-analysis of skin involvement, three for gastrointestinal outcomes, and two for muscle outcomes. The most common indications for IVIG therapy were cutaneous fibrosis, inflammatory myopathy, gastrointestinal involvement, and refractory musculoskeletal manifestations. Meta-analysis demonstrated a significant improvement in skin involvement assessed by the modified Rodnan Skin Score (SMD -0.59, 95% CI -0.95 to -0.22; p = 0.0019; I 2 = 78.0%). Gastrointestinal manifestations also improved significantly (SMD -0.73, 95% CI -1.16 to -0.29; p = 0.0012; I 2 = 0%). For inflammatory myopathies, a limited quantitative synthesis of two studies showed a significant reduction in creatinekinase levels (SMD -0.53, 95% CI -0.80 to -0.26; p < 0.001). Across studies, IVIG was well tolerated, and serious adverse events were uncommon. IVIG was associated with improvements in several clinical outcomes, particularly in observational studies, including skin fibrosis, gastrointestinal manifestations, and inflammatory myopathies. However, the only randomized placebo-controlled trial did not demonstrate significant short-term improvement in skin involvement at its primary endpoint. The available evidence suggests a potential adjunctive role for IVIG in selected patients.

items.title: Case Report: When muscle edema is not a myositis flare: Legionella pneumonia complicated by rhabdomyolysis and acute kidney injury in long-standing polymyositis.
items.abstract: Legionella pneumophila is an important cause of severe community-acquired pneumonia and can produce extrapulmonary manifestations that obscure the primary diagnosis. Diagnostic error is especially likely in patients with established idiopathic inflammatory myopathy, because fever, myalgia, weakness, creatine kinase elevation and muscle edema may be attributed to autoimmune flare. We report a 70-year-old woman with a 25-year history of polymyositis receiving long-term corticosteroids and azathioprine who developed high fever, severe bilateral thigh pain and progressive proximal weakness after recent travel. On transfer, she had anuria with bladder distension, dark urine, diffuse posterior-thigh muscle edema, pneumonia, hyponatremia, metabolic acidosis, myoglobinemia and acute kidney injury. Legionella pneumonia with rhabdomyolysis and multifactorial acute kidney injury was suspected clinically, and Legionella-active antimicrobial therapy, hydration, urinary drainage and urine alkalinization were started before microbiological confirmation. A targeted sequencing-based respiratory pathogen assay on sputum collected on Day +4 detected L. pneumophila (145 sequences; estimated concentration <10^3 copies/mL) and respiratory syncytial virus A (266,036 sequences; 10^5 copies/mL), raising the possibility of viral-bacterial coinfection. Legionella urinary antigen, targeted PCR and culture were not documented. After infection and renal injury stabilized, methylprednisolone and intravenous immunoglobulin were used because residual inflammatory myopathy activity remained in the differential. However, creatine kinase and myoglobin had already declined, so subsequent improvement cannot be attributed specifically to immunomodulation. Creatinine fell from 538 μmol/L on Day 0 to 110 μmol/L on Day +9 and 78 μmol/L on Day +30; follow-up chest CT on Day +14 showed marked improvement. This case shows that muscle MRI edema is contextual rather than etiologic. In immunosuppressed myositis patients, pneumonia plus hyponatremia, myoglobinuria and renal injury should prompt early Legionella-active treatment while autoimmune activity is reassessed after infection control.

items.title: Phenotypic characterization of patients with ANCA-associated vasculitis and diffuse alveolar hemorrhage: a data-driven analysis of a multicentre, retrospective, nationwide cohort.
items.abstract: Severe diffuse alveolar hemorrhage (DAH) is a potentially fatal complication of ANCA-associated vasculitides (AAV). This study aimed to identify distinct clinical phenotypes among patients to the ICU, and to examine their association with mortality. We conducted an ancillary analysis of the national multicenter retrospective PLEXHIA cohort, including 197 patients with severe AAV-related DAH, defined by respiratory symptoms with new infiltrates consistent with alveolar hemorrhage, along with oxygen saturation ≤85%, high-flow oxygen or mechanical ventilation requirement. Kohonen self-organizing maps were applied to predefined clinical variables at ICU admission, excluding treatment and outcomes. Clusters were interpreted and compared regarding organ involvement, severity, management, and mortality at 30 and 90 days. Between 2012 and 2024, 197 patients (66 years old, 52% female) were included, revealing marked clinical heterogeneity. Three phenotypes emerged: The MPO pulmonary-renal (MPO-PR) cluster included patients with anti-MPO ANCA, renal involvement and high oxygen requirements. The mild-respiratory (Mild-R) cluster included predominantly female patients with less severe respiratory compromise and mild renal involvement. The PR3 multi-organ (PR3-MO) cluster involved younger patients with anti-PR3 ANCA, severe acute respiratory failure and multiorgan failure. Renal replacement therapy was most frequent in the MPO-PR group (73%), while invasive mechanical ventilation was most common in the MPO-PR and PR3-MO groups (71% and 68%). Thirty-day mortality differed significantly: 23% (MPO-PR), 4% (mild-R cluster), and 14% (PR3-MO cluster). This large ICU cohort highlights three clinically relevant phenotypes of AAV-related DAH, which could inform the development of phenotype-driven immunosuppressive strategies.

items.title: Mechanistic Landscape and Therapeutic Opportunities of Non-Coding RNAs in Modulating Fibroblast-Like Synoviocytes in Rheumatoid Arthritis.
items.abstract: Current disease-modifying antirheumatic drugs (DMARDs) for rheumatoid arthritis (RA) predominantly target systemic immune-inflammatory pathways, yet fail to effectively reverse progressive articular structural damage driven by fibroblast-like synoviocytes (FLS), representing a core unmet clinical need in the field. Non-coding RNAs (ncRNAs) are key epigenetic regulators of pathological FLS activation; however, the field is constrained by three core limitations: fragmented evidence, mechanistic homogenization, and a persistent basic-to-clinical translational gap. Adopting a structured evidence-grading narrative review framework, we systematically synthesize evidence on the regulatory roles of three major ncRNA classes (microRNAs [miRNAs], long ncRNAs [lncRNAs], and circular RNAs [circRNAs]) across four hallmark RA-FLS pathophenotypes: proliferation-apoptosis dysregulation, invasive matrix degradation, pro-inflammatory secretion, and metabolic reprogramming, acting via diverse mechanisms including competitive endogenous RNA (ceRNA) sponging and epigenetic modification. We further integrated a panoramic cross-class synergistic ceRNA regulatory network and identified 12 high-confidence translational targets (prioritized by clinical, in vivo, and primary cell multi-level evidence, exemplified by miR-124, miR-146a, GAS5, and circFBXW7). We also synthesize current evidence on ncRNA biomarker utility, two canonical interventional paradigms (gain-of-function [GoF] and loss-of-function [LoF] strategies), and shared translational bottlenecks across the field. Collectively, ncRNA-targeted stroma-directed therapy emerges as a novel interventional paradigm for RA articular structural protection. Prioritized future directions include FLS subpopulation-specific functional characterization, optimization of synovial-targeted delivery systems, exploration of non-canonical regulatory mechanisms, and multicenter validation of ncRNA-based biomarkers to accelerate clinical translation.

items.title: Icariin Protects Against Mitochondrial Damage and Ferroptosis-Related Injury in Synovial Fibroblast-Like Synoviocytes Through SUMO1-Dependent Regulation of SIRT1.
items.abstract: Rheumatoid arthritis (RA) is a chronic autoimmune disease characterized by persistent synovial inflammation and progressive joint destruction, in which fibroblast-like synoviocytes (FLSs) play a central pathogenic role. Ferroptosis and oxidative stress-driven mitochondrial dysfunction have recently been implicated in synovial cell injury during RA progression. Sirtuin 1 (SIRT1), a nicotinamide adenine dinucleotide-dependent deacetylase, is known to regulate inflammation, redox homeostasis, and cell survival; however, the upstream regulatory mechanisms controlling SIRT1 function and their relevance to ferroptosis in RA remain poorly defined. Primary rat FLSs and a complete Freund's adjuvant (CFA)-induced adjuvant arthritis (AA) rat model were used. SIRT1 transcription, protein expression, subcellular localization, and enzymatic activity were assessed using quantitative real-time PCR, Western blotting, immunofluorescence, and enzymatic assays. Oxidative stress, mitochondrial dysfunction, lipid peroxidation, and ferroptosis-related parameters were evaluated using biochemical assays and fluorescence-based probes. SUMO1 expression was manipulated by knockdown and overexpression approaches, and the interaction between SUMO1 and SIRT1 was examined by co-IP.Inflammatory stimulation with IL-1β impaired SIRT1 transcriptional expression, reduced its nuclear localization, and suppressed its enzymatic activity in FLSs, accompanied by enhanced reactive oxygen species accumulation, mitochondrial dysfunction, lipid peroxidation, and ferroptosis-related changes. ICA treatment restored SIRT1 expression and activity while alleviating oxidative stress and ferroptotic injury. ICA upregulated SUMO1 expression, while Co-IP analysis demonstrated an association between SUMO1 and SIRT1. SUMO1-dependent regulation was associated with increased SIRT1 nuclear localization and enzymatic activity. Disruption of SUMO1 expression or pharmacological inhibition of SIRT1 suppressed the protective effects of ICA in FLSs. Consistent regulatory effects were observed in arthritic rats following ICA administration. These findings support the involvement of SUMO1/SIRT1 regulation in ferroptosis-related injury and mitochondrial dysfunction in RA-associated synovial cells. ICA exerts protective effects by restoring coordinated SIRT1 regulation at multiple functional levels, highlighting SIRT1-centered pathways as potential therapeutic targets for RA.

items.title: Staged multi-target therapy for anti -MDA5-positive dermatomyositis-associated rapidly progressive interstitial lung disease: a case report.
items.abstract: Anti-melanoma differentiation-associated gene 5 antibody-positive dermatomyositis-associated rapidly progressive interstitial lung disease is associated with acute respiratory deterioration and high mortality. A man in his 40s presented with fever, dry cough, progressive dyspnea, mechanic's hand-like lesions and severe hypoxemic respiratory failure. Chest high-resolution computed tomography demonstrated rapidly progressive bilateral ground-glass and reticular opacities. Myositis-specific antibody testing showed strong anti -MDA5 positivity, with concomitant anti -EJ, anti -TIF1γ and anti -Ro52 positivity. Initial intravenous methylprednisolone at 80 mg/day produced limited improvement. Early multi-target escalation included divided-dose methylprednisolone, tofacitinib, short-course intravenous immunoglobulin, Pneumocystis jirovecii prophylaxis and an individualized reduced-dose rituximab regimen consisting of 200 mg followed by three weekly 300-mg infusions. Mycophenolate mofetil was briefly withheld during acute escalation and subsequently resumed for maintenance. Oxygenation improved within 48 h, and serial imaging demonstrated progressive regression of the pulmonary abnormalities. During approximately 6.5 months of follow-up, the patient remained clinically stable without a detected serious opportunistic infection. Because several interventions overlapped and rituximab has a delayed immunological effect, the early response cannot be attributed to rituximab alone. This case illustrates the potential clinical value of staged multi-target treatment adjustment and infection-risk management in severe anti -MDA5-associated rapidly progressive interstitial lung disease.

items.title: Etanercept-Induced Cutaneous Necrotizing Vasculitis in a Patient With Rheumatoid Arthritis: A Case Report and Literature Review.
items.abstract: Tumor necrosis factor-alpha (TNF-α) inhibitors are effective therapies for rheumatoid arthritis (RA) but may rarely induce paradoxical autoimmune complications, including vasculitis. We report the case of a 53-year-old woman with seropositive RA and secondary Sjögren's syndrome who developed bilateral dependent petechial and purpuric lesions of the lower extremities after approximately 33 months of etanercept therapy at a dose of 25 mg twice weekly. At symptom onset, her RA was well controlled, with no clinical or ultrasonographic synovitis and a Disease Activity Score in 28 joints of 2.1. Skin biopsy demonstrated fibrinoid necrosis of dermal vessels, consistent with necrotizing angiitis. No gastrointestinal, renal, neurological, pulmonary, or ear, nose, and throat involvement was identified. The etiologic workup showed a normal complete blood count, preserved renal function, normal urinalysis and complement levels, negative anti-myeloperoxidase, anti-proteinase 3, anti-double-stranded DNA antibodies and cryoglobulins, and negative hepatitis B, hepatitis C, and human immunodeficiency virus serologies. Serum protein electrophoresis showed no monoclonal gammopathy. Antinuclear antibodies were weakly positive at a titer of 1:80 without clear pathological significance. Etanercept was permanently discontinued, and the active lesions resolved completely within approximately 20 days, leaving only residual hyperpigmented and cicatricial changes. No recurrence was documented during follow-up. Rechallenge was not performed, and tocilizumab was subsequently selected for RA control. The compatible latency, histological confirmation, positive dechallenge, sustained absence of recurrence, and lack of a more plausible alternative cause strongly supported the diagnosis of cutaneous necrotizing vasculitis probably induced by etanercept. This case highlights that anti-TNF-α-associated vasculitis may occur after prolonged treatment and requires systematic assessment for systemic involvement and competing autoimmune, infectious, and hematologic causes.
